paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Cross-bedding, also called cross-stratification, is layering inside a stratum that lies at an angle to the main bedding plane. The result is a roughly horizontal unit made up of inclined layers. The tilt belongs to the original layering; it was not produced by deformation after deposition. The groups of inclined layers are called cross-beds or sets, and the inclined layers themselves are called cross-strata.

paragraphs.heading: How it forms
paragraphs.text: Cross-bedding comes from bedforms such as ripples or dunes migrating downstream in a flowing fluid. The flow makes sand grains saltate up the upstream side, called the stoss side, and gather at the peak until they reach the angle of repose. At that point the crest has grown too large. The force of the moving water overcomes it, and it falls down the downstream side, called the lee side. Repeated avalanches of this kind eventually build the cross-bedding, which dips in the direction of the paleocurrent, the ancient flow.

paragraphs.heading: Where it turns up
paragraphs.text: Cross-bedding can form in any setting where a fluid flows over a bed of material that can move. It is most common in stream deposits made of sand and gravel, in tidal areas, and in aeolian dunes. Its presence shows that the place where the sediment was deposited had a flowing medium, typically water or wind.

paragraphs.heading: Reading direction, with a catch
paragraphs.text: The direction in which the beds dip indicates the paleocurrent, the rough direction in which sediment was carried. The layers that form on the downstream side of the bedform are called foresets. Foresets are laid down at the angle of repose, about 34 degrees from the horizontal, so geologists can measure their dip direction and calculate the direction of the old flow. There is a catch. Most cross-beds are troughs, and troughs can give a 180 degree variation in the dip of foresets, so measuring foresets blindly can give a false paleocurrent. In that case the true direction is found from the axis of the trough.

paragraphs.heading: Two main types
paragraphs.text: The two types described most often are tabular and trough cross-bedding. Tabular cross-bedding has units that extend a long way horizontally compared with the thickness of the set, and their bounding surfaces are essentially planar. It forms mainly as large-scale, straight-crested ripples and dunes migrate, and it forms during lower-flow regimes. In trough cross-bedding the bounding surfaces are curved, and so the units are limited in horizontal extent.

paragraphs.heading: Size and how to spot it
paragraphs.text: A single cross-bed can be just a few tens of centimeters thick or as much as hundreds of feet or more, depending on the depositional environment and the size of the bedform. Each foreset can be told apart from the next because material of different sizes and densities is separated, on a small scale, into different layers. Where the set is less than 6 centimeters high and each layer is just a few millimeters thick, geologists say cross-lamination instead.
